library(fpp2)
## ── Attaching packages ──────────────────────────────────────────── fpp2 2.5.1 ──
## ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ fma       2.5  
## ✔ forecast  9.0.2     ✔ expsmooth 2.3
## 
library(readxl)
busineesforecasting_us_average_prices_monthly <-read_excel("busineesforecasting_us_average_prices_monthly.xlsx")

#Creating a subset of the original dataset to filter the items to only be eggs since there are multiple different items to look at. I picked eggs specifically because their price has been talked about a lot recently. 
eggs <- subset (busineesforecasting_us_average_prices_monthly, grepl("egg", item, ignore.case=TRUE))

#Looking to see the class of the subeset It returns "data.frame" so we have to tell R it is a time series 
class(eggs)
## [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
#Making the egg subset into a time series 
ts_eggs <-ts(eggs$price,start = c(2015,1),frequency = 12)
#Created ts_eggs by taking the egg subset and the price column. The start = c (2015,1) is when the time series starts since the first record is from Jan 2015 and the frequency is 12 for 12 months. Ran class(ts_eggs) to check it is now a time series and I will be using it for the rest of the code. 

attributes(ts_eggs)
## $tsp
## [1] 2015.000 2026.417   12.000
## 
## $class
## [1] "ts"
plot(ts_eggs)

#This output shows how the price of eggs (ts_eggs) changes over time, on a yearly basis. There was a high peak in 2025, which could of been effected by the US economy at that time. Even during COVID in 2020 the prices were not as high.

Acf(ts_eggs)

#This graph shows the price of eggs compared to a month lag. There is a strong correlation of prices between the shorter month lags.   


#Taking the mean using all of the available history
mean_forecast <- meanf(ts_eggs,5)
plot(mean_forecast)

#This shows the mean forecast 5 months into the future. The egg price appears to level off.  





# Naive forecast. This shows a forecast for the price using the last price and keeping it the same for the next 5 months. 
naive_forecast <- naive(ts_eggs,5)
plot(naive_forecast)

# Random Walk creates a forecast using the current months price and forecasting by increasing that price for the next 5 months
rwf_forecast <- rwf(ts_eggs,5)
rwf_forecast <- rwf(ts_eggs,5, drift=TRUE)
plot(rwf_forecast)

# Seasonal Naive assumes that the price will be the same that month as the year prior. March 2025 price = March 2024 price.
snaive_forecast <- snaive(ts_eggs,5)
plot(snaive_forecast)

#Creating the moving averages of 5 months and 9 months
MA5_forecast <- ma(ts_eggs,order=5)
MA9_forecast <- ma(ts_eggs,order=9)

#Plotting all of the charts into one single chart
plot(mean_forecast)
lines(naive_forecast$mean,col="red")
lines(rwf_forecast$mean,col="green")
lines(snaive_forecast$mean,col="black")
lines(MA5_forecast,col="Pink")
lines(MA9_forecast,col="Blue")

#This chart shows all of the forecasts plotted together. You can see the Snaive forecast (black line) is higher than the rest of them because it is forecasting a seasonality trend where those months will equal those months from the year prior. That is not really accurate since there is no seasonality. 
 
#The attributes of the naive forecast
attributes(naive_forecast)
## $names
##  [1] "method"    "model"     "lambda"    "x"         "fitted"    "residuals"
##  [7] "series"    "mean"      "level"     "lower"     "upper"    
## 
## $class
## [1] "forecast"
#Decomposition
ets_forecast <- ets(ts_eggs)
plot(ets_forecast)

attributes(ets_forecast)
## $names
##  [1] "loglik"     "aic"        "bic"        "aicc"       "mse"       
##  [6] "amse"       "fit"        "residuals"  "fitted"     "states"    
## [11] "par"        "m"          "method"     "series"     "components"
## [16] "call"       "initstate"  "sigma2"     "x"         
## 
## $class
## [1] "fc_model" "ets"
ets_forecast$mse
## [1] 0.07455282
#This graph shows us the level, slope, and observed trends. The observed line is the actual data from the data set. The level shows the overall movement of the data, since the level is not much different than the observed we can tell the model is smoothing the data. For the slope, above 0 = prices are increasing, below 0 = prices are decreasing, near 0 = little/no change. Around 2016, we see a negative trend, showing the prices were decreasing. There is a really high peak around 2025 that falls. There is no seasonality in this data set. 


#HoltWinters Model
HW_forecast <- HoltWinters(ts_eggs)
plot(HW_forecast)

SSE_Simple <- HoltWinters(ts_eggs,beta=FALSE,gamma=FALSE)
attributes(SSE_Simple)
## $names
## [1] "fitted"       "x"            "alpha"        "beta"         "gamma"       
## [6] "coefficients" "seasonal"     "SSE"          "call"        
## 
## $class
## [1] "HoltWinters"
plot(SSE_Simple)

SSE_Simple$SSE
## [1] 10.94024
head(SSE_Simple$fitted)
##              xhat    level
## Feb 2015 2.113000 2.113000
## Mar 2015 2.088001 2.088001
## Apr 2015 2.132998 2.132998
## May 2015 2.065003 2.065003
## Jun 2015 1.962004 1.962004
## Jul 2015 2.569975 2.569975
#The SSE is 10.94 which measures the total forecasting error for the historical data. Trend and seasonality are excluded in this so the model is assuming that the egg prices are determined by the current level rather than the long term trend. 

#Forecast
forecast_ets_1 <- forecast.ets(ets_forecast, h=5)
plot(forecast_ets_1)

forecast_ets_2 <- forecast(ets_forecast, h=5)
plot(forecast_ets_2)

#Checking the accuracy of all of the forecasts
accuracy(mean_forecast)
